paragraphs.heading: No zero from nonzero
paragraphs.text: An integral domain is a commutative ring, other than the zero ring, in which multiplying two nonzero elements never gives zero. Integral domains generalize the ring of integers and give a useful setting for studying divisibility. In a ring R, a divides b when ax = b for some x in R. The units are the elements that divide 1, and these are exactly the invertible elements.

paragraphs.heading: Several equal definitions
paragraphs.text: There are several ways to say the same thing. An integral domain is a commutative ring, not the zero ring, without nonzero zero divisors. Equivalently, every nonzero element can be cancelled: if a ≠ 0 and ab = ac, then b = c. Another version asks that for each nonzero r, the map sending x to xr be injective; elements with this property are called regular. Finally, an integral domain is a ring isomorphic to a subring of a field, and each one can be embedded in its field of fractions.

paragraphs.heading: Some variation in words
paragraphs.text: The definition is almost the same everywhere, but not quite. Some authors do not require an integral domain to have a multiplicative identity. Noncommutative versions are sometimes allowed, though the much more usual habit keeps "integral domain" for the commutative case and says "domain" when noncommutative rings are included. Some sources, Lang in particular, say entire ring instead.

paragraphs.heading: Examples
paragraphs.text: Polynomial rings are integral domains when their coefficients come from one. So ℤ[x], the polynomials in one variable with integer coefficients, qualifies, as does ℂ[x₁, …, xₙ]. Formal power series over an integral domain form one too. So do the holomorphic functions on a connected open subset of the complex plane, and every regular local ring. For any integer n that is not a square, the ring ℤ[√n] is an integral domain.

paragraphs.heading: Rings that fail
paragraphs.text: Several familiar rings are not integral domains. In ℤ/mℤ with m composite, write m = xy with neither factor equal to 1 or m; then x and y are nonzero, yet xy is 0. In a product of two nonzero commutative rings, (1, 0)⋅(0, 1) = (0, 0). Square matrices of size 2 or more fail as well: if the image of N lies inside the kernel of M, then MN = 0.

paragraphs.heading: A link to geometry
paragraphs.text: Taking quotients by prime ideals gives more examples. The quotient ℂ[x, y]/(y² − x(x − 1)(x − 2)), which corresponds to a plane elliptic curve, is an integral domain, and this can be checked by showing that y² − x(x − 1)(x − 2) is irreducible. By contrast, for a field k and non-constant polynomials f and g, the quotient by (fg) is not one, because the images of f and g are nonzero but multiply to 0. Geometrically, this means the zeros of fg generally form an algebraic set that is not irreducible.
